passage:
Every first Sunday, Nkechi makes her mum's jollof rice in the tiny flat kitchen in Leeds, and every first Sunday she lets the bottom burn a little, on purpose.
"That crispy layer was the best bit," she tells Hana, scraping it into two bowls.
Six years ago she couldn't walk past the rice aisle. In her second year, when she still couldn't sleep or make it to lectures, her GP pointed her to a bereavement counsellor, and those Thursday sessions are part of why she can stand at this stove now.
Today she laughs telling Hana how her mum sang loudly and badly while stirring. Her eyes sting halfway through the story, and she lets them.
Later she video-calls her brother in Lagos to argue about how much pepper is too much, then goes back to her thesis draft. Her mum would have wanted it finished.

qa.q: What does Nkechi cook every first Sunday?
qa.a: Her mum's jollof rice, with the bottom left to burn a little on purpose.

qa.q: What shows that Nkechi now feels warmth as well as pain when she remembers her mum?
qa.a: She laughs telling Hana about her mum's loud, bad singing, yet her eyes sting halfway through and she lets them.

qa.q: What helped Nkechi when her grief stayed stuck, and why did it matter?
qa.a: When she still couldn't sleep or get to lectures, her GP pointed her to a bereavement counsellor, and those sessions helped her reach the point where the recipe brings warmth.

qa.q: What might the first-Sunday cooking mean for Hana?
qa.a: Hana gets to know Nkechi's mum through the crispy rice and the stories, and sees a friend carry on with life while keeping the memory close.

grounding: Shows years-later grief held with warmth through a kept recipe, alongside earlier counselling when the pain had stayed frozen.

At the community centre in Dehradun, the last child packed up her geometry box, and Sahil stayed back, wiping the whiteboard slowly.
Dolma, who runs the Saturday library next door, leaned in. "You always stay late. Why?"
"My father did," Sahil said. "He taught maths at a government school for thirty years and never left while a kid still had a doubt. He died when I was eighteen."
"Is it hard, doing his thing?"
"It was. For two years I couldn't even open his notebooks. The college counsellor helped me get unstuck." He smiled. "Now when a kid finally gets fractions, it's like he's in the room. It stings a bit and feels good at the same time."
Dolma nodded. "Six years is a long time to keep someone that close."
"He's in how I teach," Sahil said, capping the marker. "That's enough."

What does Sahil mean when he says it 'stings a bit and feels good at the same time'?
qa.a: He feels both the ache of missing his father and warmth that his father's way of teaching lives on through him.

qa.q: What helped Sahil when his grief was stuck, and what could someone in that place do?
qa.a: When he couldn't open his father's notebooks for two years, the college counsellor helped him get unstuck; anyone frozen like that could reach out to a counsellor too.

qa.q: How are the children at the centre affected by Sahil's habit?
qa.a: They get a teacher who stays until their doubts are cleared, so they benefit from his father's value without knowing its story.

grounding: Illustrates a continuing bond years after a death, kept alive through a parent's value, with counselling having helped earlier when grief was stuck.
